Ad hoc translation from "*Die verhängnisvolle Anmaßung: Die Irrtümer des Sozialismus*" (1988) by Friedrich A. Hayek. See the German text [here](http://www.misesde.org/?p=13183)

The term "social", which makes every other word after it completely lose all meaning, finds its, by far, worst usage in the almost globally used term "social justice". Even though I have already discussed it quite comprehensibly in the second volume of my trilogy *Recht, Gesetzgebung und Freiheit (Die Illusion der sozialen Gerechtigkeit)*, I must briefly discuss it here because it plays such an important role in the arguments for and against socialism.

The term "social justice" is, as a well-respected man with much more courage than me said a long time ago, nothing more than "semantic treachery of the same kind as popular democracy" (Curran, 1958: 8). The alarming extent to which this term has already misled the thinking of the younger generation is shown by a dissertation from Oxford about *Social Justice* (Miller, 1976) in which the common image of justice is being referred to in a highly unusual remark: "There seems to be a category of private justice."

I have also read the remark that "social" means everything which reduces or eliminates differences in income. But why should such acts be "social"? Maybe because they are methods to secure majorities, ie. additional votes on top of those which you would already get through other means? This might be true, but that would also mean that every call for "social" behavior is a call for more steps towards the "social justice" of socialism.

Thus, the usage of this term "social" is practically the same as the call for "justice in distribution". This is incompatible with competition and with the growth or even the maintenance of the population number and wealth. Through such follies, men got far enough as to consider "social" the largest obstacle towards the maintenance of a "society". Instead of social, it should be really called "anti-social".

It is probably true that the people would be happier with their economic situation if they had the impression that the relative positions of individuals were just. But the entire idea of justice in distribution - that the individual should receive what he morally deserves - is nonsensical in the order of human cooperation (the economy) because the available product (its size, even merely its existence) depends on a morally indifferent method of distribution of its pieces.

Moral behavior cannot be determined objectively and, in every case, adjusting the big picture towards facts which have yet to be determined requires that we agree with the statement: "Success is based on results, not on motives" (Alchian, 1950: 213). Every expanded system of cooperation must continuously adjust itself to the changes of its natural environment (including the life, health, and strength of its members); the demand that the only changes which should happen are those with a just result is ridiculous. It is almost as ridiculous as the belief that the deliberate organization of a reaction to such changes could be just.

Without inequality - which is neither being influenced by deliberate moral judgement nor would be compatible with it - mankind would have never been able to reach its current size, nor would it be able to maintain it today. Performance will, of course, improve the chances of the individual, but by itself cannot ensure results.

The envy of those who underwent the same efforts is quite understandable, but it goes against the common interest. If the common interest is *really* our interest, then we must not surrender to this quite humane instinctive reaction, but we must hand over the act of rewarding to the market mechanism. Other than the market, nobody can judge the size of a contribution of an individual to the total product, and nobody else could judge how much remuneration would have to be offered to someone so that he can pick the profession by which the total available stream of goods and services would grow by the largest amount. If this profession would be also considered morally good, then the market would have created an extraordinarily moral result.

Through promises which cannot be realized, mankind is split in two hostile camps. [Any compromise between these camps] cannot get rid of the causes of this conflict, because, with every concession to misinterpreted facts, only more unrealizable expectations get created. Yet, an anti-capitalist ethic is growing and blooming on the fertile ground of false opinions of men who resent the wealth-creating institutions which are responsible for their existence.

Under their "love of freedom", they condemn exclusive property, freedom of contract, competition, advertisement, profit, and even money itself. By surrendering to the illusion that their reason could tell them how human labor should be used to better serve their innate desires, they have become a severe threat to civilization.
The worst use of the word "social" is in "social justice"
